Atlas/Chemistry

The material world · ABOUT 20 MINUTES

Same atoms. Wildly different stuff.

Rusting armour, cooking food and burning fuel all involve matter changing. Chemistry asks what things are made of, how their atoms are arranged and what happens when they react.

START WITH A QUESTION

A steel tank rusts. Has some of its metal simply disappeared — or has something joined it?

Have a guess together before revealing the idea.

The idea underneath +

Everything around you is made of atoms. Elements contain one type of atom; compounds have different types chemically joined. In an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into new substances. They are not created or destroyed, even when gases escape and the change looks mysterious.

Why know this?

Chemistry helps explain cooking, cleaning, batteries, fuels and why materials fail. It helps you distinguish a change of shape or state from the formation of a new substance.

01

Armour has an enemy: air

Iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water to form rust. The corrosion can weaken the metal.

02

Why explosions are so sudden

Some reactions transfer energy and produce expanding gases very quickly. The rate matters as well as the amount of energy.

03

Materials built for a job

A ceramic mug, a polymer helmet shell and a metal pan behave differently because of their materials and structures.

THINK / DRAW / TRY

Make it a conversation.

Use two colours of coins or paper circles as atoms. Build a few pretend molecules, then rearrange them into different groups without adding or removing any pieces. Count before and after. This models conservation of atoms, not which reactions are actually possible.

One more twist

An ice cube melts. A piece of iron rusts. Which makes a new substance, and how could you tell?

Help me explain this +

Rust contains iron combined with oxygen and other components, so iron has not vanished. A retained rust sample includes material from the surroundings; flakes falling away can complicate a real weighing. Listen for “atoms rearrange” and for a distinction between a new substance and a new state.

A common mix-up

Dissolving does not mean disappearing. Dissolved material is still present, even when you cannot see it.

Think like a scientist

If a reaction seems to lose mass, what would you need to collect or contain to test where the matter went?
